analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy rules to teens 13-15 and bans targeted ads to them.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with one bipartisan cosponsor in March 2019 but never received a Senate committee hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill updates a 1998 law that protects children's data online. It would extend those protections to teenagers ages 12 through 16, require websites and apps to get consent before collecting their personal information, ban targeted advertising aimed at children and most advertising aimed at teens, give families the right to see and delete data collected about them, and ban sale of internet-connected toys and devices aimed at kids unless they meet cybersecurity standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents of young children and families with teenagers. Today, federal online privacy law only protects children under 13; this bill would give 13-to-15-year-olds the right to consent to (or block) collection of their personal data, request deletion of what companies hold, and escape advertising profiles built from their browsing. Families buying connected toys and gadgets would get a privacy label on the box explaining what data the device collects.

how_it_helps.text: Extends to 13-to-15-year-olds ('minors') privacy protections that previously applied only to children under 13, covering notice, consent, and deletion rights [S2] [S3].
Bans targeted marketing to children outright, and bans targeted marketing to teens unless the teen gives verifiable consent [S2] [S3].
Gives parents and teens the right to request a description of what personal information a company holds, delete it, and challenge inaccurate information [S2] [S3].
Bars companies from making app or game participation conditional on handing over more personal information than is needed to play [S3].
Requires a standardized privacy dashboard on the packaging of connected devices aimed at children and teens, and bans sale of such devices that fail FTC cybersecurity standards [S2] [S3].
Prohibits using children's personal information to direct content based on race, socioeconomic factors, or proxies for them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Online platforms, app makers, and the digital advertising industry, which would lose the ability to profile and target ads to users under 16 without consent, and connected-device manufacturers, which would face new security and labeling requirements. Some compliance costs could ultimately be passed to consumers, and ad-supported 'free' services might reduce features for teen users.
analysis.who_pays_short: Adtech firms, platforms, and device makers

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on companies of all sizes. Small app developers and website operators directed at children would face FTC rulemaking deadlines, consent-verification systems, and deletion mechanisms that large platforms are far better equipped to absorb [S3].

The bill requires age verification before serving mixed-audience users, which means collecting more information from everyone in order to determine who is a minor — an ironic cost the bill acknowledges in its own safe-harbor construction for mixed-audience services [S3].

Section 10 requires operators of sites directed at children to treat every user as a child unless the FTC allows otherwise, which could restrict adult use of child-oriented services and push companies to redesign or exit the kids' market entirely [S3].
The bill relies on FTC rulemaking for most of its specifics, so the actual protections would depend on regulations written over the following years rather than on the statute itself [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: stronger privacy and less surveillance advertising for young people versus compliance costs and fewer targeted-ad-funded free services. The bill includes industry-friendly features — self-regulatory 'safe harbors' where companies can write their own guidelines subject to FTC approval — that an honest critic could call a loophole, and its reliance on slow rulemaking means benefits would arrive gradually. Still, the protections for teens' data are substantive and the costs fall mainly on firms whose business model is profiling young users.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read once, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill on March 12, 2019, joined by Sen. Hawley as cosponsor [S1] [S4] [S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — is recorded for the remainder of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms and the targeted-advertising industry kept the ability to collect and profile data on users under 16 without the consent requirements this bill would have imposed; connected-device makers avoided new security and labeling mandates. Families and teens gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online platforms and the adtech industry

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend children's online privacy protections to teenagers and add targeted-advertising bans and device security rules.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Online platform and digital advertising industry
against.role: Major commercial interests affected by the bill
against.what_they_did: Companies whose revenue depends on collecting and targeting user data generally opposed expanding children's privacy mandates during this era; the record itself shows no floor action was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat from Massachusetts and a Republican from Missouri — but with only two senators behind it and no recorded committee or floor votes, its partisan shape in the chamber was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would ban compiling or using minors' personal information for targeted marketing without the minor's verifiable consent, and ban it outright for children. Targeted advertising built on profiling young users is the industry's core revenue mechanism.

industries.industry: Social media, websites, and app operators
industries.note: Operators directed at children or minors would need verifiable consent to collect data, provide deletion and correction rights, and stop conditioning participation on data collection — costs that reduce the data available to ad-funded platforms.

Devices aimed at kids would need FTC cybersecurity standards, security-update commitments, and a privacy dashboard on the packaging. Compliance raises costs, though verifiable security claims could help sales to safety-conscious parents.
